Most aspirants mug up “Places in News” like facts.

UPSC doesn’t ask facts.
It asks connections.
Let’s test yours 👇

1. Red Sea
Rift-origin sea between Africa and Arabia, connects Mediterranean to Indian Ocean via Suez and Bab-el-Mandeb, critical global oil trade route with unique high-salinity coral ecosystems

2. Luzon Island (Philippines)
Largest island of Philippines, lies between South China Sea and Pacific, volcanically active (Mt. Pinatubo), key to Indo-Pacific geopolitics and typhoon impacts

3. Greenland
World’s largest island in Arctic, massive ice sheet driving sea-level rise, rich in rare earths, emerging hotspot in US-Europe-China strategic competition

4. Baltic Sea
Shallow brackish sea in Northern Europe, limited water exchange, surrounded by NATO countries, hosts pipelines and cables making it geopolitically sensitive

5. Iran
Strategically located in West Asia, controls Strait of Hormuz through which major global oil passes, tectonically active with deserts and mountain ranges

6. Muna Island (Indonesia)
Located in Wallacea zone, known for limestone karst, caves and prehistoric art, represents transition between Asian and Australian biodiversity

7. Victoria (Australia)
Southeastern state with temperate climate, facing intense bushfires due to climate change, includes Great Dividing Range and fertile yet fire-prone plains

8. Iraq
Located in West Asia, dominated by Tigris-Euphrates river system, fertile Mesopotamian plains amidst desert, rich in oil and central to regional geopolitics

9. Venezuela
Northern South America, major oil reserves around Lake Maracaibo, diverse geography from Andes to Llanos plains and Orinoco basin, ongoing territorial tensions

10. Weimar Triangle
France-Germany-Poland grouping formed post-Cold War, coordinates EU security and diplomacy, significant in shaping Europe’s response to Russia-Ukraine conflict

11. Black Sea
Enclosed sea between Europe and Asia, crucial for Russia-Ukraine war dynamics, controls grain exports and naval access via Bosphorus

12. Horn of Africa
Includes Somalia, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Djibouti, located near Bab-el-Mandeb, critical maritime chokepoint with piracy and geopolitical competition

13. South China Sea
Highly contested region with overlapping claims, artificial islands, rich fisheries and hydrocarbons, vital for global shipping lanes

14. Arctic Ocean
Rapidly warming polar region, opening Northern Sea Route, rich in untapped resources, emerging arena of global power competition

15. Sahel Region
Semi-arid belt south of Sahara, facing desertification, coups and insurgency, important for climate-security nexus

If you’re just reading names, you’ll forget.
If you connect geography, IR, and environment, you’ll solve questions.
Now do this
Take a blank world map and mark all these places.

That one exercise will give you more clarity than hours of reading.

From Japan to the Philippines — history just thundered across Luzon. 🇯🇵🇺🇸🇵🇭

For the first time ever, Japan deployed its Type 88 Surface-to-Ship Missile system to the Philippines for live-fire training during Balikatan 26 in Laoag. Side by side with Filipino and American forces, this exercise sends a powerful message:

The Indo-Pacific stands united.  
Prepared.  
And ready to defend peace.

More than missiles and military drills, this is about trust, partnership, and a shared commitment to protect freedom and stability in our region. As tensions continue to rise, allied nations are proving that cooperation is our strongest defense against any attempt to change the status quo by force.

Three nations. One mission.  
Peace through strength.

#BK2026 #Balikatan #ShoulderToShoulder #Japan #UnitedStates #Philippines

War History Online:
Herman Davis was born on January 3, 1888, in Manila, Arkansas. A quiet man from a small farming community, Davis didn’t seek attention or fame. But his reputation as a skilled marksman made him stand out even before  World War I. When the U.S. entered the war in 1917, Davis, at almost 30  years old, decided to enlist. Though he could have avoided combat duty because of his age and height (he was a bit under the typical size  requirements), he went straight into service, joining Company I of the 113th Infantry Regiment, 29th Division.
Davis  quickly proved himself during his training with a Springfield rifle, impressing his superiors with near-perfect accuracy. Sent to the front lines in France, he found himself fighting in some of the war’s most intense battles. One of his most famous feats took place at the  Battle of Belleau Wood in 1918. During this fierce battle, Davis spotted a German machine gun nest firing on his comrades from a range of about 1,000 yards. With open sights and no fancy scopes, Davis calmly aimed his Springfield rifle and took out five enemy soldiers, effectively silencing the gunner. Afterward, when others praised him, he humbly called it “just a good shootin' distance,” brushing it off as if it were  nothing special.
Another story that solidified Davis’s reputation came from his role in the  Meuse-Argonne Offensive. This massive offensive, one of the last of the  war, took place in September and October 1918. During one particularly  intense engagement, Davis went ahead of his squad under heavy fire and  took out several German snipers who were hidden and targeting American soldiers. This act saved lives and allowed his unit to move forward.
Davi  was awarded the Distinguished Service Cross for his actions in the  Meuse-Argonne. Additionally, his bravery caught the attention of the French government, which awarded him the Croix de Guerre and the  Médaille Militaire for his valor in battle. Despite these honors, Davis kept his head down, never boasting about his feats. When he returned to Arkansas after the war, he didn’t seek recognition or parades. Locals  eventually learned about his deeds, and a statue was raised in his honor in his hometown.
Herman Davis lived quietly after the war, but his health declined, partly due to the toll of wartime exposure to gas. He died of tuberculosis on  January 5, 1923, just two days after his 35th birthday.
